_procedure: Why this file exists, and the order it has to happen in: extract the semantics, disambiguate the English, identify the genuine terms of art, set a translation policy for each — and only THEN generate locales. Skip to a locale and a linguistically perfect translation can be functionally nonsense, because most of this vocabulary is ordinary English carrying a domain meaning. The question a translator should be handed is never 'what does warp mean in French', it is 'what would a French-speaking stone author call a field that distorts the whole slab's geometry, specifically not textile warp'.
_note: Translator glossary. Read this BEFORE translating any pack. Most of these are ordinary English words carrying a domain meaning, so a confident wrong reading produces a translation that looks fine and is wrong. `means` is what Stone Author means. `notThe` is the reading to avoid — usually the first one a dictionary gives. `ruling` is keep (leave the English term), translate, or trade (use your language's established stone/glass/masonry term, and if it genuinely has none, keep the English rather than coin one — a mason searching for an invented word finds nothing). IMPORTANT: where a hint names an equivalent in another language it is a CANDIDATE TO VERIFY against a trade source, never a ruling. These were written from general knowledge, and at least one was wrong on first pass (point de Hongrie was offered for herringbone when it is the mitred pattern). Trust the `means` and the `notThe` — that is what the implementation does. Treat the foreign-language suggestions as leads.

gauge.means: the thickness of a drawn vein across its width
gauge.notThe: a measuring instrument, a pressure gauge, or a railway gauge
gauge.hint: the sense is line weight / stroke thickness

family.means: a named set of stone characters (Carrara, Calacatta, Nero Marquina, Granite) that decides how veins rough, swell and branch
family.hint: closer to 'type' or 'variety' of stone than to kinship

ground.means: the base stone material lying UNDER all the authored structures and inclusions — the base bucket (base colour, clouds, banding, breccia, fog). Its colour is the whole slab's fill
ground.notThe: electrical earth, the floor, coffee grounds, or the slab's visible top SURFACE — Stone Author has a real depth model and 'surface' means the polished coat on top (specular, lens), which is the opposite end of the stack
ground.hint: the painter's sense of a ground: the material you build on top of. Prefer your language's word for base/background material over any word meaning surface

matrix.means: the fine-grained rock surrounding the angular fragments in a breccia
matrix.notThe: a mathematical array or a grid
matrix.hint: geological sense; many languages keep a cognate of matrix/matrice here

island.means: a ZONE where the warp is held off, so the stone inside stays undistorted while the rest of the slab deforms. The effect is graded, not binary: full inside the radius, easing off across the feather, so the edge of an island is partly affected by design. Since the inverse sense was added, an island can also be turned inside out — a zone that is the ONLY place the warp acts
island.notThe: a landmass in water, or a kitchen island
island.hint: the metaphor is deliberate and worth keeping if your language supports it. Say ZONE or REGION, not disc: the drawing primitive is a disc today, but islands compose — several overlapping ones make a zone of any shape — and nothing in the idea requires a circle

warp.means: a field that distorts the whole slab's geometry
warp.notThe: the lengthwise threads in weaving, or faster-than-light travel

moon.means: a tool that warps the geometry as if a gravitational body had passed through it — you drag the body across the slab and the stone deforms in its wake
moon.notThe: a month, a lunar phase, or anything to do with lunar imagery
moon.hint: use your language's ordinary word for the celestial moon. The name is not decorative: the tool models a mass with gravity, so the astronomical word is the correct one. Do NOT rename it after what it does (a 'drag tool' or 'smudge tool') — that loses the model

web.means: a network of fine cracks spreading from a line
web.notThe: the World Wide Web or a web page
web.hint: the sense is a spider's web / a craquelure network

identity.means: a view that paints every authored ARTIFACT in its own colour so each can be told apart — one mark is one artifact whatever its sub-lines, and it covers web cracks, specks and drusy as well as veins
identity.hint: the sense is 'which object is which', not 'which line is which' — do not narrow it to lines, because it identifies non-line artifacts too

pour.means: a tool that pours material onto the slab in a flowing stream

chip.means: to knock a small corner off a tile edge
chip.notThe: a silicon chip, or a potato chip

seam.means: in Stone Author this always refers to a STYLOLITE seam: the thin, toothed, dark parting left where rock dissolved under pressure. It is one of the three things you can select with Tune (a vein, a web crack, or a seam), and 'Seam width' on the Stylolite panel is its thickness
seam.notThe: a sewing seam, a weld seam, or a seam in the mining sense of a workable deposit (a coal or ore seam) — that is a layer you would extract, whereas this is a dissolution surface. The geological family is right; the specific thing is not a deposit
seam.hint: the word for a thin planar parting or discontinuity in rock, not for a bed or deposit

angle.means: a view that colours each speck by the direction it points
angle.notThe: a point of view or an opinion

fold.means: geological folding — how much a vein buckles back on itself
fold.notThe: folding paper, or folding in cooking

spectrum.means: the scalar value the light sits at, from -1 to 1, where 0 is daylight. Each artifact carries a LIST of activation entries (a value and a colour) and lights only when the light's value falls within a tolerance of one of them — otherwise it does not emit at all and goes dark against the black ground. So sweeping the spectrum makes different sets of artifacts appear AND disappear; it is an observation state, not a brightness control
spectrum.notThe: a political spectrum, or a vague 'broad range'
spectrum.hint: the optical sense. Avoid any word suggesting intensity or amount — the value selects WHICH artifacts are observable, it does not scale how strongly they glow

bucket.means: one of the five groups a layer is EXPORTED into (base, web, micro, minor, major). The studio's many authoring layers collapse into these five on the way out, and a layer's bucket is independent of where it sits in the render order
bucket.notThe: a pail, or a paint-bucket fill tool
bucket.hint: the sense is category or bin — which output file a layer ends up in, not where it is drawn

light.means: both the illumination of the slab and the Light tool that aims it

height.means: on the MAGNET panel: how far above the slab the magnet is held. Lower means a sharper fan of specks around the pole. It is a distance in the third dimension, above the stone
height.notThe: the slab's height or the height of anything drawn on it. Note the Stylolite panel's separate 'Tooth height', which IS an amplitude in the plane of the slab — these two are different quantities sharing one English word
height.hint: the sense is elevation / standoff distance, how far off the surface the tool is

reach.means: the radius around the pointer within which a tool has any effect at all; outside it, nothing happens
reach.notThe: reaching for something, or the reach of an argument
reach.hint: the sense is radius of influence / range

strength.means: how intensely a tool acts within its reach
strength.notThe: physical strength, or the strength of a material
strength.hint: the sense is intensity of the effect, not the toughness of the stone

hover.means: in 'hover traces': letting a pen or mouse work on the slab from ABOVE, without contact — the tool still acts, at reduced strength
hover.notThe: a hover state in a user interface, i.e. the mouse merely being over something
hover.hint: the physical sense of holding the tool off the surface. It is an authoring mode, not a UI state

comb.means: as a verb, what the magnet does when laid over: draws specks into parallel alignment along the direction the pen leans
comb.notThe: a comb for hair, as a noun
comb.hint: the verb sense of combing fibres or filings into parallel order

tilt.means: how far the pen is leaned over from upright, read from the stylus. On the magnet it sets the magnet's AXIS: upright fans the specks from the pole, laid flat combs them along the lean. On a vein it softens the edge
tilt.notThe: tilting a screen, or a pinball tilt

pressure.means: how hard the pen is pressed, read from the stylus. It sets a vein's width and a pour's flow; on the magnet it brings the magnet CLOSER to the slab
pressure.hint: stylus pressure, as in a graphics tablet

slab.means: a cut panel of stone, here 8x5 ft
slab.hint: the stone trade's word for a cut panel: lastra (IT), dalle/tranche (FR), Platte (DE)

vein.means: a mineral-filled fracture running through the stone

stylolite.means: a serrated, toothed seam formed where rock dissolved under pressure
stylolite.hint: an international geological term with direct cognates: stylolithe (FR), Stylolith (DE), stilolite (IT), estilolito (ES)

boudinage.means: a layer stretched until it breaks into sausage-shaped segments
boudinage.hint: already French and used untranslated in geology worldwide

en-echelon.means: parallel segments each offset from the last, like a row of steps
en-echelon.hint: already French and used untranslated in structural geology

breccia.means: rock made of angular fragments cemented together
breccia.hint: already Italian; most languages use a cognate (brèche FR, Brekzie DE, brecha ES)

clast.means: one angular fragment inside a breccia

drusy.means: a surface lined with a crust of tiny sparkling crystals
drusy.hint: Druse (DE), druse/geode (FR/IT); if your language has no adjective, describe the crystal crust

dendritic.means: branching repeatedly like a tree or a frost pattern

halo.means: an ALTERATION HALO — the zone of host rock around a mineral vein that the vein chemically altered and bleached as it formed. Rendered as a wide, soft, low-opacity band painted UNDER the vein in a lightened version of its colour, concentric with it
halo.notThe: a drop shadow, or a halo in the religious/decorative sense. A drop shadow is offset, darker, and implies a light direction; this is centred on the vein, LIGHTER than it, and implies no light at all — it is a feature of the rock, not a graphical effect on top of it. If it must be compared to a graphics effect, an outer glow is the closer one
halo.hint: use the geological term if your language has one (alteration halo / alteration zone around a vein); otherwise a word for a surrounding bleached or altered band

speck.means: one small mineral grain in granite. A speck has an ORIENTATION (an axis) but no direction — the renderer treats both ends as the same thing, which is why the Angle view can colour it by how it lies
speck.hint: the sense is a fleck or grain, not a dot of dirt

magnet.means: a tool whose physical model is a BAR MAGNET held over a bed of iron filings: the pointer is the magnet, the granite specks are the filings. It ROTATES specks where they already lie — it does not move them. (Gravity is the tool that moves them.) Held upright the field leaves the pole and the specks fan out radially from it; laid over, the field combs them along the way the pen leans, and the two blend continuously with the lean. Alignment builds with TIME over a spot, so a slow pass aligns harder than a flick
magnet.notThe: a fridge magnet, a magnetic personality, or a magnet in the sense of attracting things toward a point — nothing is pulled anywhere
magnet.hint: use the physics word for a bar magnet. The single most important thing to preserve is ROTATES, not attracts or moves: a translation implying attraction describes Gravity instead

filings.means: iron filings — the metaphor for how granite specks behave under the magnet, arranging themselves along the field
filings.hint: the classroom-demonstration sense, iron filings on paper over a magnet

gravity.means: a tool that MOVES specks: tap for a point, drag for a line. Pull gathers them into clusters or bands, push clears a space. The counterpart to the magnet, which rotates them instead
gravity.notThe: the seriousness of a situation, or gravity as a general physical constant
gravity.hint: the attracting-mass sense. Keep the contrast with the magnet legible: this one changes WHERE specks are, the magnet changes HOW THEY LIE

align.means: the magnet's forward mode: rotate specks toward the field's axis, so they come to lie the same way

scatter.means: the magnet's reverse mode: break existing alignment up, randomising how specks lie. Also the button that re-rolls a granite layer's speck positions
scatter.notThe: scattering as in light scattering — that is a different part of the studio (subsurface, back light)
scatter.hint: two distinct uses of the same English word; both are about disorder in ARRANGEMENT, neither is optical

kerf.means: the width of material removed by a cutting process along its path — the material LOSS between the two resulting edges. Sawing, abrasive waterjet, laser and plasma cutting all produce a kerf, so it is not specific to a blade
kerf.notThe: the cut itself, the cut path, or the line the tool follows. The kerf is the material that is gone, measured across the path — not the path
kerf.hint: a real trade term, not general English. It must denote the WIDTH or the material loss; a term meaning 'cut line' or 'saw line' is wrong even where the trade uses it loosely. Candidates to verify: Schnittfuge / Schnittbreite (DE) are the gap and the width, both fine; a literal 'trait de scie' (FR) names the saw and the line, so prefer something like largeur de coupe; spessore di taglio (IT) is the thickness of cut. In Stone Author it is why veins drift slightly across every tile joint — that drift IS the lost material

grout.means: the filler in the gap between laid tiles

subsurface.means: light TRANSPORT inside the stone: light enters the surface, scatters within the material and comes back out, which is what makes marble read as translucent rather than painted. It describes what happens to light inside the stone, not where the light comes from
subsurface.hint: the rendering term (subsurface scattering); many languages keep the English in technical contexts. Keep it clearly DISTINCT from back light — a translator reaching for 'lit from within' will collide with that separate control. They are separate render passes and cannot both apply

backlight.means: illumination arriving from BEHIND the slab, as if it were held up to a window. Each layer blocks it according to its own transmittance, folded from the deepest layer upward
backlight.notThe: a screen's backlight, or a rim light behind a subject
backlight.hint: the sense is transillumination — light passing THROUGH the stone from the far side. The companion term is subsurface, which is about light scattering INSIDE the stone; name the source here, not the scattering

transmittance.means: how much light a layer lets through when back-lit — 0 is opaque, 1 is clear. Veins are nearly opaque, specks semi-opaque, the matrix passes light
transmittance.hint: the optical term. The control is labelled 'pass' in the Selected bar for brevity; translate that label for what it means, not the English word 'pass'

emission.means: a colour an artifact gives off by itself at a particular spectrum value, rather than a colour it reflects. An artifact may carry several, each activating at a different value
emission.hint: the physical sense, as in emission spectrum — self-luminous, not illuminated

spotlight.means: makes the light a beam of a given radius, so an artifact must be inside the beam as well as matched to the spectrum before it lights
spotlight.notThe: public attention or a figurative spotlight
spotlight.hint: the stage or torch sense; it adds a spatial condition on top of the spectral one

specular.means: mirror-like reflection; here, how polished the surface reads

fresnel.means: a lens whose surface is cut into concentric stepped rings
fresnel.hint: named after Augustin-Jean Fresnel — a proper noun, never translated

reeded.means: glass moulded into parallel rounded vertical ridges

herringbone.means: a tile pattern of rectangles with SQUARE ends laid at right angles to each other, so the rows step
herringbone.notThe: chevron, where the tile ends are mitred so the rows meet in a continuous unbroken V. They are different patterns and the trade distinguishes them
herringbone.hint: name the square-ended pattern. Candidate to verify: Fischgrat (DE), spina di pesce (IT). In French, bâtons rompus is this pattern and point de Hongrie is the MITRED one — do not use point de Hongrie here

basketweave.means: a tile pattern of pairs laid alternately across and along

cairo.means: a tiling of identical irregular pentagons, named after Cairo
cairo.hint: a proper noun in the name of the tiling

subway.means: a tile pattern of offset rows of regular rectangles
subway.hint: use whatever that pattern is actually called in the language. The English name is incidental — it comes from New York subway tiling — so do not translate the word 'subway'; name the pattern
